1840:
Blasphemy is the act of speaking, writing, or behaving in a way that deeply disrespects, insults, or shows contempt for something considered sacred — most commonly God, a religion, holy figures, or sacred objects.

Think of it this way: every religion has things it holds as the most sacred and untouchable — God's name, holy prophets, scripture, divine symbols. Blasphemy is when someone attacks, mocks, or insults those things at their very core.

The word is a noun, so it refers to the act itself or an instance of that act. You can say:

  • "That was blasphemy." (referring to a single act)
  • "He was accused of blasphemy." (the offense/charge)
  • "Blasphemies filled the book." (multiple instances)

The person who commits blasphemy is called a blasphemer. The adjective form is blasphemous (meaning "of the nature of blasphemy"). The verb is to blaspheme.

Blasphemy can take many forms:

  • Spoken words — cursing God, denying God's existence in a mocking or contemptuous way, or saying something deeply offensive about a prophet or holy figure.
  • Written words — publishing text that ridicules or degrades sacred beliefs.
  • Actions or gestures — desecrating a holy book, defiling a religious symbol, or performing an act that mocks a sacred ritual.
  • Art or images — depicting God, prophets, or holy figures in a disrespectful or degrading way.

The key ingredient in all of these is contempt or disrespect directed at something a group holds divinely sacred. It is not just disagreement — it goes further into mockery, insult, or deliberate desecration.
A Very Important Nuance: Blasphemy Is Relative

Here is something crucial to understand: what counts as blasphemy depends entirely on the religion or belief system in question.

  • Something that is deeply blasphemous in Islam might not be considered blasphemous at all in Buddhism.
  • Something offensive to Christians may be perfectly acceptable in a secular (non-religious) worldview.
  • Even within the same religion, different groups may disagree on what crosses the line.

This means blasphemy is not an objective, universal fact — it is a judgment made from within a particular faith. A person outside that faith may not even recognize that they have said or done something blasphemous.

These words are related but mean different things:

Blasphemy vs. Criticism of religion
Criticizing a religion's practices, history, or teachings is not automatically blasphemy. Blasphemy specifically targets the sacred and divine — God, prophets, holy texts — with contempt or mockery. A scholar saying "this religious institution made historical mistakes" is criticism. Someone saying something deeply contemptuous about God or a prophet is blasphemy.

Blasphemy vs. Heresy
Heresy is holding a belief within a religion that contradicts the official teachings of that religion. It is an insider problem — a Christian believing something the Church calls doctrinally wrong is a heretic. Blasphemy, on the other hand, is about disrespecting the sacred and does not require you to be a member of that religion. An outsider can commit blasphemy.

Blasphemy vs. Sacrilege
Sacrilege is the violation or misuse of something sacred — like stealing from a church or using holy objects for mockery. It leans more toward physical desecration of sacred things or places. Blasphemy leans more toward speech and expression that insults the divine. The two overlap but are not identical.

Blasphemy vs. Profanity
Profanity (swearing, cursing in everyday speech) is crude or offensive language in general. Blasphemy is a specific sub-type — when that offensive language is directed at God or the sacred. Saying a random swear word is profanity. Saying something contemptuous about God is blasphemy. All blasphemy involving speech is a form of profanity, but not all profanity is blasphemy.

Historically, blasphemy was treated as one of the most serious offenses imaginable in deeply religious societies. In medieval Europe and in many theocratic kingdoms, blasphemy was punishable by death, torture, or exile, because insulting God was seen as an attack on the entire social and moral order.

Many countries still have blasphemy laws on their books — laws that make it a criminal offense to insult or defame God, prophets, or religion. These laws are especially active in several countries in the Middle East, South Asia, and parts of Africa. Punishments can range from fines to imprisonment to, in the most extreme cases, execution.

In contrast, many Western countries (like the United States, France, and most of the European Union) have moved away from blasphemy laws, prioritizing freedom of speech and freedom of expression. In these places, blasphemy is not a crime — though it may still be considered deeply offensive and morally wrong by religious communities.

This creates an ongoing global tension: the religious community's right not to have their sacred beliefs insulted versus the individual's right to express themselves freely.
Why Does Blasphemy Feel So Serious to Believers?

To understand why blasphemy provokes such strong reactions, you have to understand what the sacred means to a believer. For a deeply religious person, God is not just an idea — God is the source of all existence, truth, goodness, and love. Prophets are not just historical figures — they are divinely chosen messengers. Scripture is not just a book — it is the literal or inspired word of God.

When someone mocks or insults these things, a believer does not just feel offended in their opinion the way you might feel offended by someone insulting your favorite food. They feel that the very foundation of reality, morality, and meaning has been attacked and degraded. This is why, across history, blasphemy has provoked responses ranging from grief and outrage to violence.

Blasphemy is the act of speaking, writing, or behaving in a way that shows deep disrespect or contempt for God, holy figures, sacred texts, or religious symbols. It goes beyond simple disagreement or criticism — it involves mockery, insult, or desecration of what a faith community considers divine and untouchable. What qualifies as blasphemy varies by religion and culture. It is distinct from heresy (wrong belief within a religion), sacrilege (physical desecration), and general profanity (crude language). Historically and in many parts of the world today, blasphemy is treated as a serious offense — sometimes even a crime — while in more secular societies it is protected as free expression, even if considered morally wrong by believers.
1841: "Blast" is a rich word with several distinct meanings. Think of it as a word that captures the idea of something sudden, powerful, and forceful — whether that's air, sound, fire, or even emotion. Here is every meaning explained clearly.
1. A Sudden, Powerful Rush of Air or Wind

The most basic meaning of blast is a strong, sharp burst of air that hits you suddenly.

It's different from a gentle breeze. A blast is short, sudden, and hits you with force — like a punch of air.

Examples:

  • When she opened the freezer, a blast of cold air hit her face.
  • A blast of hot wind swept across the desert.
  • The workers were nearly knocked over by the blast from the jet engine.

Think of it this way: if wind were a person, a breeze would tap you on the shoulder, but a blast would shove you.

A blast is also a violent explosion — the kind caused by a bomb, dynamite, or any explosive force. This includes both the physical explosion itself and the wave of pressure and heat that spreads outward from it.

Examples:

  • The blast from the gas explosion shattered windows a mile away.
  • Rescue workers searched the rubble after the deadly blast.
  • The soldiers were trained to take cover from a blast.

The key feeling here is destruction through sudden release of energy. A blast in this sense is dangerous and powerful.

Extending from the idea of a rush of air, blast can refer to a forceful stream of any substance — air, steam, water, smoke, or even sand — that is deliberately directed or shoots out with power.

Examples:

  • The mechanic used a blast of compressed air to clean the engine.
  • A blast of steam shot out from the broken pipe.
  • The firefighters directed a blast of water at the burning building.

Here, the "blast" is more controlled than an explosion, but it still carries the idea of something coming out with great force.
4. A Loud, Sharp Burst of Sound

A blast can be a sudden, loud, sharp sound — especially from a horn, whistle, trumpet, or siren. It is not a long, continuous sound. It is short and startling.

Examples:

  • A blast of the ship's horn echoed across the harbor.
  • The referee gave a sharp blast on his whistle to stop the game.
  • A blast from the truck's horn warned the cyclist to move aside.

Think of the difference between music flowing from a violin versus a single, sharp honk from a car horn. The honk is more like a blast — abrupt and attention-grabbing.
5. A Powerful Hit, Shot, or Kick

In informal and sports contexts, a blast means a very hard, powerful strike — a hit, kick, punch, or shot delivered with maximum force.

Examples:

  • The striker sent a blast of a shot into the top corner of the net.
  • The batter hit a blast that sailed over the outfield wall for a home run.
  • The boxer landed a blast to his opponent's ribs.

The emphasis here is on raw power — not a gentle tap, but a full-force strike.
6. A Sharp, Forceful Verbal Attack or Criticism

A blast can also be used figuratively to describe a sudden, aggressive criticism or verbal attack on someone or something. Just as a physical blast hits hard and fast, a verbal blast is a fierce outburst of words aimed at someone.

Examples:

  • The newspaper published a blast against the government's handling of the crisis.
  • Her speech was a full-on blast at her rivals in the party.
  • The coach's post-match blast at his players left the dressing room silent.

The connection to the physical meanings is clear: words, like an explosion or a gust of air, can be directed at someone with great force.

In casual, everyday conversation, blast is used to describe something that is extremely fun and exciting. This is one of the most common informal uses of the word, especially in American English.

Examples:

  • The road trip was an absolute blast — we laughed the whole time.
  • "Did you enjoy the concert?" "It was a total blast!"
  • The kids had a blast at the birthday party.

Think of the excitement and energy of an explosion — something so thrilling that it feels like a burst of energy and joy. That's the feeling this meaning captures.

This is an extremely common phrase built from this word, and you will encounter it often.

"At full blast" means at maximum power, volume, or speed — with nothing held back.

Examples:

  • The air conditioner was running at full blast during the heatwave.
  • She had her music playing at full blast and couldn't hear the doorbell.
  • The factory's machines were working at full blast to meet the deadline.

The image is simple: like an explosion or a rush of air at its most powerful — no limits, nothing reduced, everything going as hard as it can.

At the heart of every meaning of blast is a single unifying idea: a sudden, powerful force. Whether it is air, an explosion, sound, a strike, a criticism, or even a feeling of joy — a blast is never mild or quiet. It always carries a sense of intensity, energy, and impact.

MeaningThe Core Idea
Rush of airA hit of powerful wind
ExplosionA violent burst of force
Stream of substanceDirected, powerful flow
Loud soundA sharp, startling noise
Hard strikeA full-force hit
Verbal attackFierce, sharp criticism
Great funAn explosion of joy and excitement
At full blastMaximum power, no limits

Once you understand this core idea — sudden, powerful force — every meaning of blast will feel natural and make complete sense in context.
1842:
When you describe someone as blasé, you are saying they are unimpressed, indifferent, or unbothered by something — not because the thing is genuinely boring, but because they have experienced it so many times that it has lost its ability to excite or impress them anymore.

It describes a very particular kind of "I don't care" attitude — one that comes specifically from over-familiarity and over-exposure.
The Key Ingredient: Why They Feel That Way

This is the most important thing to understand. Being blasé is not plain boredom. The word has a very specific cause baked into it:

A person is blasé because they have had so much of something good, exciting, or impressive that they can no longer feel the thrill of it.

Think of it like this. The first time a child tastes ice cream, their eyes go wide with joy. But if that child somehow ate ice cream every single day for five years, eventually they would shrug at it. "It's just ice cream." That shrug — that flat, unimpressed attitude born from having had too much of something — is being blasé.

So the word carries a built-in story: I have seen this. I have done this. I have had this. Many, many times. It no longer moves me.

A blasé person, when faced with something that would excite most people, reacts with:

  • A shrug
  • A flat, unimpressed expression
  • Little to no emotional reaction
  • A calm, almost bored tone

Imagine a celebrity who gets invited to fancy parties every single weekend. When a friend excitedly tells them, "We're going to a rooftop party with a live band and a five-star chef!" — the celebrity just goes, "Oh. Sure." No excitement. No enthusiasm. Not because they are ungrateful, but because this is just... Tuesday for them.

That celebrity is being blasé.

The word carries a slight undertone of world-weariness and, sometimes, a whisper of arrogance or snobbery. When someone is described as blasé, there is often an implied sense that they feel they are above being impressed — that they have moved through the world so much and experienced so many things that ordinary people's thrills no longer reach them.

This is why the word is not entirely neutral. Calling someone blasé can be:

  • Descriptive — simply noting that they are unimpressed (e.g., "She was blasé about the whole awards ceremony.")
  • Mildly critical — suggesting they are being dismissive or taking something for granted (e.g., "He was frustratingly blasé about his own incredible achievement.")

Context tells you which one is meant, but the word almost always carries a faint flavour of "this person has seen too much to be moved."

• "The seasoned travel journalist was completely blasé about the five-star hotel — she had stayed in dozens just like it."
    → She wasn't impressed. Too many five-star hotels in her past.
  • "Teenagers can often seem blasé about things their parents find remarkable."
    → Over-exposed to so much stimulation, they're hard to impress.
  • "He tried to look blasé at the party, but you could tell he was actually nervous."
    → He was performing indifference — pretending to be too cool to care.
  • "Don't be so blasé about your health — just because you feel fine now doesn't mean you should ignore the warning signs."
    → Here, it's used critically: stop being carelessly indifferent.

Sharpening a word means knowing its edges. Blasé is not:

  • Sad or depressed. A blasé person isn't suffering — they're just flat and unmoved.
  • Angry or resentful. There's no hostility in it. It's calm indifference.
  • Lazy. Blasé is about emotional reaction, not effort.
  • Simply bored. Regular boredom can happen to anyone in any situation. Blasé specifically comes from overexposure to something — usually something that others would find impressive or pleasurable.

If you ever want to check whether blasé fits, ask yourself:

"Is this person unimpressed or indifferent because they've had too much of a good or exciting thing?"

If yes — blasé is your word.
1843:
When something is blatant, it means it is so completely obvious and out in the open that it is impossible to miss — and it is done without any shame, guilt, or attempt to hide it.

Those two ideas — shocking obviousness and shamelessness — are both packed inside this single word. If either one is missing, "blatant" is probably the wrong word.

Think of blatant as having two layers:

Layer 1 — It's impossible to miss.
Something blatant is not subtle. It's not hidden in the background. It is right there, in your face, completely out in the open. Anyone with eyes and a brain can see it instantly.

Layer 2 — It's done without shame or disguise.
The person doing it isn't even trying to hide it, deny it, or feel bad about it. There is a boldness — almost an arrogance — to it. It's as if they don't care that everyone can see what they're doing.

Together, these two layers create the full meaning: openly, shamefully, obviously wrong — and making zero effort to conceal it.
An Important Pattern: Blatant Almost Always Describes Something Negative

This is critical to understand. "Blatant" is almost never used to describe something good, neutral, or harmless. It nearly always accompanies something that is wrong, dishonest, unfair, disrespectful, or offensive.

You will hear and read it paired with words like:

  • a blatant lie
  • a blatant mistake
  • a blatant violation
  • blatant disregard (for rules or people)
  • blatant discrimination
  • blatant hypocrisy
  • a blatant attempt (to cheat, manipulate, etc.)
  • a blatant contradiction
  • a blatant foul (in sports)

The negativity is almost always present. Using "blatant" to describe something positive would sound very strange and would usually be sarcastic or humorous.

"Blatant" sits at the extreme, high-intensity end of the scale of obviousness. Compare:

  • noticeable → mild, easy to spot
  • obvious → clear and apparent
  • glaring → very obvious, hard to ignore
  • blatant → so obvious it's almost offensive; no attempt whatsoever to hide it

So when you say something is blatant, you're not just saying "I noticed it." You're saying "this is so glaringly, shamelessly out in the open that it's almost shocking."

Here are clear, real-life examples to show how the word works:

  1. "That was a blatant lie."

He didn't just lie — he lied openly, confidently, and without a hint of shame, even when everyone around him knew the truth.

  1. "The referee missed a blatant foul."

The foul was so obvious — so clear to every single person watching — that it was shocking the referee didn't call it.

  1. "The company showed a blatant disregard for its workers' safety."

They didn't even pretend to care. They broke safety rules openly, without any attempt to cover it up or make excuses.

  1. "She made a blatant attempt to copy his answers during the exam."

She didn't hide it. She turned her head, looked at his paper, and wrote down his answers — right in front of the teacher. No effort to be secretive at all.

  1. "The new policy was a blatant contradiction of everything the president had promised."

The contradiction was so clear and obvious that no one could possibly miss it or argue otherwise.
How It's Used in a Sentence (Grammar)

As an adjective, "blatant" can appear in two positions:

Before a noun:
"It was a blatant lie."
Here, "blatant" directly describes the noun "lie."

After a linking verb (like "is," "was," "seems"):
"The hypocrisy was blatant."
Here, "blatant" comes after the verb and still describes the subject, "hypocrisy."

Both are correct and common.

Several words are close to "blatant" but not identical:

Obvious — something is easy to see or understand. But "obvious" has no built-in sense of shamelessness or wrongness. A solution to a math problem can be "obvious." It cannot be "blatant."

Glaring — focuses on how impossible something is to miss, like a bright light in your eyes. A "glaring error" is a very visible mistake. But "glaring" doesn't carry the shamelessness angle the way "blatant" does.

Brazen — focuses on the shameless boldness of a person. A person can be brazen. An action can be brazen. But "blatant" puts more emphasis on the visibility of the thing, while "brazen" puts more emphasis on the attitude of the person doing it.

Flagrant — this is the closest word to "blatant." A flagrant act is also openly and shamelessly wrong. However, "flagrant" tends to carry a stronger sense of moral outrage and is often used in legal or formal contexts (e.g., "flagrant foul" in basketball, "flagrant violation of human rights"). "Blatant" is a bit more general and everyday.
One Subtle Nuance: It Often Implies Insult to the Audience's Intelligence

When something is blatant, there is often an implied insult: the wrongdoer is acting as if you're too blind or too foolish to notice — or they simply don't care what you think. This is part of why "blatant" carries an emotional sting. It's not just "this is obvious." It's "this is so openly wrong, and they're not even trying to pretend otherwise."
A Simple Way to Remember It

Whenever you're unsure whether "blatant" fits, ask yourself two questions:

  1. Is it completely obvious — impossible to deny or overlook?
  2. Is it negative, and done without any shame or attempt to hide it?

If both answers are yes, "blatant" is almost certainly the right word.
1844:
Blatantly means doing something in a way that is completely open and obvious — with no attempt to hide it, no shame, and no care for what others think. It almost always describes something that is wrong, bad, or inappropriate.

Think of it as two ideas fused into one word:

Completely obvious + Done shamelessly = Blatantly

Imagine someone cheating on a test. There are different ways they could do it:

  • They might secretly peek at a classmate's paper — looking left and right, hiding it carefully.
  • They might quietly glance over when the teacher turns away.
  • Or they might just openly turn and copy their classmate's entire paper, in full view of everyone, without even flinching.

That third person is doing it blatantly. They are not hiding it. They are not embarrassed. They don't seem to care at all. The act is sitting right there in the open for everyone to see.
The Two Parts You Must Understand

1. It Is Obvious — Impossible to Miss

When something is done blatantly, there is zero subtlety. It is not hidden, not disguised, not even slightly covered up. Anyone who looks can see it immediately and clearly.

2. It Is Shameless — Done Without Guilt or Care

This is what separates blatantly from simply saying "obviously." The person doing the thing shows no embarrassment, no guilt, no effort to justify themselves. They act as if there is nothing wrong, even when there clearly is.

This combination — being obvious and shameless at the same time — is the heart of the word.
Why It Almost Always Describes Something Negative

Blatantly is almost never used for good or neutral things. You would not say "she blatantly helped her friend" or "he blatantly studied hard." Those are positive or neutral actions — they don't need this word.

Blatantly is reserved for things that are wrong, unfair, rude, dishonest, or inappropriate. The word itself carries a feeling of disapproval and shock. When you use it, you are signaling that the action was not just visible — it was audacious. It had a kind of nerve to it.

It is a strong word. It does not mean "a little obvious" or "somewhat shameless." It means completely, undeniably, and boldly done in the open. When someone uses "blatantly," they are saying there is no room for doubt. The thing was right there, in plain sight, for everyone to witness.

Here are different examples so you can see how the word works in real situations:

1. Lying:
"He blatantly lied to his boss about finishing the report."
→ He did not hesitate. He did not look guilty. He just looked his boss in the eye and said something false, openly and without shame.

2. Ignoring rules:
"She blatantly ignored the 'No Parking' sign and left her car there for hours."
→ The sign was right in front of her. She saw it. She parked anyway. No attempt to pretend she didn't notice.

3. Copying:
"The new company blatantly copied their competitor's product design."
→ The copy was so obvious that anyone could see it. And the company did not even try to disguise it.

4. Rudeness:
"He blatantly stared at her food the entire meal without saying a word."
→ He did not try to be subtle. He just stared, openly, making it obvious and uncomfortable.

5. Unfairness:
"The referee blatantly favored the home team throughout the match."
→ Everyone watching could see the bias. It was not a matter of interpretation — it was clear and undeniable.
How "Blatantly" Feels Different from Similar Words

Obviously just means something is easy to see. It is neutral.
"She obviously worked hard on this." → Fine, no negativity.

Blatantly means something is easy to see and done shamelessly, usually referring to something wrong.
"She blatantly copied this work." → Disapproval is built in.

Openly means without hiding, and can be positive or neutral.
"He openly shared his feelings." → That's actually admirable.

Blatantly can also mean without hiding, but always carries a sense of wrongness or audacity.
"He blatantly lied." → Shocking and wrong.

So while these words are related, blatantly is the one that packs in both the idea of full visibility and the moral judgment that the person should know better — but doesn't seem to care.
When Should YOU Use This Word?

Use blatantly when:

  • Someone does something wrong or inappropriate in a way that is completely visible to everyone.
  • The person shows no guilt, no hesitation, and no attempt to hide what they are doing.
  • You want to express shock or disapproval at how open and shameless the action was.

A quick test: before using "blatantly," ask yourself two questions —

  1. Is this action clearly visible and impossible to deny? ✓
  2. Is it also something wrong or inappropriate, done shamelessly? ✓

If both answers are yes, "blatantly" is the right word.
One Final Way to Remember It

Picture someone doing something wrong right in front of your face, with a straight expression, making absolutely no effort to hide it. That image — the openness, the shamelessness, the audacity — is exactly what blatantly means.
1845: To blate means to make a bleating sound — the weak, wavering cry that a sheep, lamb, or calf makes. Think of a young lamb calling out to its mother: that soft, trembling "baa" is what blating sounds like.

At its most literal, you blate when you cry out in the way a sheep or calf does. It's not a loud, powerful sound. It's thin, shaky, and slightly helpless.

The lamb blated from the other side of the fence.

Here is where the word gets richer. When used about a person, blate carries the same qualities — weakness, whininess, and a lack of conviction. It describes someone who speaks or cries in a feeble, plaintive, or foolishly rambling way. The implication is almost always slightly dismissive: the person is not saying anything powerful or worth listening to; they are just making noise, much like a lost, helpless animal.

Stop blating about your problems and do something about them.

The picture it paints: imagine someone whimpering, complaining, or muttering weakly without purpose — not a strong, reasoned argument, just ineffectual noise.
The single feeling the word captures

Blate as a verb captures a very specific quality of sound and speech: weak, wavering, and a little pitiful. Whether it's an animal or a person, the one doing the blating is not strong, bold, or commanding. They are making a thin, trembling appeal into the air — and nobody is particularly moved by it.

This is a rare, dialectal word — mainly found in Scottish English and some older British dialects. You will not hear it in everyday modern conversation. However, you may encounter it in older literature, dialect poetry (particularly Scottish), or rural writing. When you do, the meaning will always orbit that same idea: a weak, bleating, whining kind of utterance.
Quick summary to lock it in

ContextWhat "blate" describes
  • Animal: the bleating cry of a sheep, lamb, or calf.
  • Person: speaking or crying in a weak, whining, or foolishly rambling way.
  • Tone: always slightly dismissive — the sound has no real strength or purpose behind it.

If you remember just one image: a lost lamb calling out softly and uselessly in a field — that is the heart of blate.
1846:
Blather is long, rambling talk or writing that sounds like a lot is being said, but when you really pay attention, almost nothing meaningful is there. It's words and sentences that fill up time and space without delivering any real substance, insight, or value.

Think of it this way: if you listen to someone speak for ten minutes and walk away thinking "what was the point of all that?" — that was blather.

Three things usually come together:

1. It's excessive. Blather isn't a single pointless sentence. It's a stream — a flood of words that just keeps going. The person speaks at length, in great volume, often with energy and confidence.

2. It's empty. Beneath all those words, there is very little actual content. No real idea is being developed. No useful information is being shared. No argument is being made. It's the verbal equivalent of a bag full of air — it takes up space, but there's nothing inside.

3. The speaker doesn't usually notice. The person producing blather is typically unaware that their words are hollow. They aren't lying or trying to trick you. They're simply talking without genuine substance, often because they enjoy the sound of their own voice, or because they want to appear knowledgeable without really being so.
Blather vs. words that seem similar

It helps to understand what blather is not, or how it differs from related ideas:

  • Nonsense is talk that is logically confused or makes no sense — the ideas themselves are incoherent. Blather might actually be logically structured; you can follow the sentences. It just doesn't lead anywhere worth going.
  • Gibberish is hard to understand at all — like someone speaking in a language you don't know, or stringing random sounds together. With blather, you understand every word. The problem isn't clarity; it's pointlessness.
  • A lie is deliberate deception. Blather isn't deceptive — the person isn't trying to mislead you. They're just talking without real depth or purpose.
  • Small talk is light, casual conversation (like chatting about the weather). It may not be deep, but it serves a social purpose — it's friendly and connecting. Blather lacks even that usefulness; it's more self-indulgent.

When someone is speaking blather at you, you often feel a particular kind of frustration — a slow, creeping impatience. You keep waiting for the point to arrive, and it never does. You feel your time is being wasted. There's a sense that the speaker is in love with talking, but not really saying anything. Listeners sometimes describe it as being "talked at" rather than talked to.

Blather is often used with a tone of mild contempt or weary exasperation:

  • "I tried to ask him a simple question, but I got twenty minutes of blather."
  • "The meeting was full of corporate blather — no decisions, no clarity, just buzzwords."
  • "She tuned out his blather and stared out the window."
When and where the word is used

"Blather" is informal — you'd use it in everyday speech or casual writing, not in a formal report. It has a slightly humorous, exasperated edge to it. It's not a harsh insult, but it is dismissive. If you call someone's speech "blather," you're expressing that you found it tiresome and worthless, but without necessarily being cruel about it.

It is commonly used to describe:

  • Long-winded political speeches full of vague promises and no real policy
  • Corporate or bureaucratic language that sounds official but says nothing concrete
  • A person who talks too much without ever arriving at a point
  • A rambling conversation that goes in circles

To cement your understanding, here are words that are close in meaning, each with a slightly different shade:

  • Drivel — similarly empty talk, but with a stronger sense of stupidity or foolishness
  • Twaddle — silly, trivial talk, often from someone who thinks they're being profound
  • Waffle — especially used in British English for vague, indecisive talk that avoids committing to anything
  • Hot air — talk that is boastful and empty, full of promises or grand claims with nothing behind them
  • Balderdash — nonsensical talk, but with a more comic or old-fashioned feel

All of them share the core of blather: much said, little meant.
One sentence to remember it by
If you want a single mental anchor: blather is the noise people make when they're talking without thinking, or thinking without much to say.
1847:
To blather means to talk at great length in a foolish, empty, or pointless way. When someone blathers, they keep going on and on, producing a stream of words that carry little to no real value. The listener is typically left bored, mildly irritated, or just waiting for the talking to stop.

Think of it like a tap left running — water keeps flowing, but it isn't filling anything useful.

For speech to qualify as blathering, it generally needs all three of these:

1. A lot of talking. Blathering is never brief. It implies prolonged, continuous talking — someone who blathers doesn't make their point and stop; they just keep going.

2. Empty or foolish content. The words being spoken are either nonsensical, trivial, or simply useless. There's no real substance to what's being said.

3. No meaningful point. The person doesn't seem to be building toward any useful conclusion. They're not informing you, persuading you, or helping you. They're just... talking.

This is where the word gets interesting. Blather is not a neutral word. When you say someone is blathering, you are quietly dismissing them. You are signaling: "I don't think what this person is saying has any value."

Equally important: the person who is blathering is almost always unaware that they're being tiresome. They're not embarrassed; they're not holding back. They just keep going, completely unbothered. This obliviousness is part of what makes the word mildly contemptuous.

That said, it's a soft dismissal — not a harsh insult. It has a mildly exasperated, eye-rolling quality to it, rather than genuine anger. You'd use it in casual, everyday conversation. It would feel out of place in formal writing.
How Blather Differs from Similar Words

These words are often confused with blather, but each has its own flavour:

Ramble — To ramble means to talk in a disorganized, wandering way, jumping from topic to topic without a clear path. Someone who rambles might actually have something worthwhile to say, but they can't stay focused. Blathering implies the content itself is foolish or worthless, not just disorganized.

Babble — To babble focuses on the sound of speech being rapid, unclear, or jumbled (think of a baby babbling). Blathering is specifically about the content being empty or silly, not about how the words sound.

Prattle — To prattle is to talk in a childlike, light, or trivially cheerful way. It's often used for children or for harmless chit-chat. Blathering is more dismissive and implies a greater level of foolishness.

Drone on — To drone on means to speak in a dull, monotonous tone for a long time. Blathering doesn't require a dull tone at all — someone can blather loudly and enthusiastically. The difference is that "drone on" is about how it sounds; blathering is about how meaningless it is.

Reading a word in real sentences is often the fastest way to truly understand it:

  • "Stop blathering and just answer my question."
  • "He blathered on for half an hour without saying anything useful."
  • "She asked him what time dinner was, and he started blathering about the history of cooking."
  • "The politician blathered nonsense for the entire interview."
  • "I couldn't get any work done because my colleague kept blathering about his weekend."
  • "Don't blather — I have five minutes. Just give me the key points."

You'll very commonly see "blather on" — the word "on" reinforces the sense that it just keeps going and going, with no end in sight.

You'll also see "blather about" — which tells you the (typically unimportant) subject of the blathering.

These two can combine: "He was blathering on about his car troubles for an hour."
A Note on Register and Usage

Blather is used predominantly in informal, spoken, everyday English. It has particularly strong roots in British and Irish English, where it has been used for a long time, but it is well understood and used throughout the English-speaking world.

It can be used about someone in the third person ("He just blathers"), or directed at someone ("Stop blathering!"), or even used self-deprecatingly ("Sorry, I'm blathering again" — though this is rarer, since blathering implies a lack of self-awareness).
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: to blather = to talk a lot, foolishly, and pointlessly — without realizing (or caring) that you're wasting everyone's time.
1848: Blaze captures the idea of something that is intensely bright, vivid, and impossible to ignore. Whether it is fire, light, color, or emotion — a blaze is never quiet or subtle. It is always powerful, striking, and demanding of attention.
All the Meanings, One by One

1. A Large, Bright, Fierce Fire

This is the most common meaning. A blaze is a fire that is not just burning — it is burning strongly, brilliantly, and with great heat. It is bigger and more intense than an ordinary flame.

The firefighters struggled to control the blaze that had spread across three buildings.

Campers sat around the blaze, warming their hands.

Key nuance: The word "blaze" suggests a fire that is roaring and alive, not a small, quiet flame. A single candle is not a blaze. A burning forest is.

2. A Burst or Flood of Bright Light

A blaze can also be a sudden, overwhelming amount of light — not necessarily from fire. Think of how the sun can hit you like a wall of brightness when you step outside.

She walked out of the dark tunnel into a blaze of sunlight.

The stage was lit in a blaze of white spotlights.

Key nuance: The light is not gentle. It floods, overwhelms, and fills the space entirely.

3. A Brilliant Display of Color

When color is extremely vivid, rich, and eye-catching — almost as if it is glowing — it can be called a blaze of color.

The autumn trees were a blaze of red, orange, and gold.

The garden was a blaze of color after the spring rains.

Key nuance: The colors are not just pretty — they are so vibrant and intense that they almost feel warm, like fire.

4. A Sudden, Powerful Burst of Emotion or Activity

A blaze can describe a sudden, explosive outburst of feeling — such as anger, passion, or enthusiasm. The emotion comes on fast and burns intensely, just like a fire.

He left the room in a blaze of fury.

The announcement was met with a blaze of excitement from the crowd.

Key nuance: The emotion is not slow or gradual. It flares up suddenly and with great force. This is why "blaze" works so well here — fire and strong emotion feel similar in their sudden, consuming power.

5. A White Mark on an Animal's Face

In a completely different and very specific sense, a blaze is a white stripe or patch running down the center of an animal's face, especially a horse or a dog.

The brown horse had a distinctive white blaze running from its forehead to its nose.

I recognized our dog immediately by the blaze on her forehead.

Key nuance: This is a very literal, physical marking. It is called a "blaze" because the bright white patch stands out sharply against the darker fur or coat — like a flash of light on the animal's face.

6. A Mark Cut on a Tree (Trail Marking)

A blaze can also be a mark — usually a cut, notch, or painted spot — made on a tree to guide travelers along a path through a forest or wilderness. Hikers and explorers have used this method for centuries.

Follow the blazes on the trees and they will lead you back to the campsite.

The old blaze on the oak tree was nearly overgrown after all these years.

Key nuance: This meaning is closely connected to the phrase "blazing a trail," which means to mark a new path for others to follow — and by extension, to do something new and pioneering. Even in this physical sense, a blaze is a clear, visible marking that stands out.

7. "Blazes" — Used as an Exclamation

The plural form blazes is used in certain informal and slightly old-fashioned expressions to show strong surprise, frustration, or disbelief. In this context, "blazes" is a mild, dramatic substitute for a stronger word.

What in blazes is going on here?

Where in blazes did I put my keys?

Key nuance: This usage treats "blazes" almost as a way of invoking fire and chaos to express how shocking or confusing something is. It adds emphasis and emotion without using strong profanity.
What Ties All These Meanings Together

Even though these meanings seem very different on the surface, they share a common thread:

A blaze is something that stands out sharply and powerfully. Whether it is a roaring fire, blinding light, vivid color, explosive emotion, a white stripe on a horse, or a mark on a tree — a blaze is never dull, hidden, or easy to miss.

Think of it this way: if something blazes, it announces itself. It cannot be overlooked.
Common Phrases Using "Blaze" as a Noun

A blaze of glory — A dramatic, impressive ending or achievement. Doing something in a spectacular, memorable way right before it ends.

The retiring athlete finished in a blaze of glory, winning the championship in her final game.

In a blaze of publicity/media attention — When something receives a sudden, overwhelming amount of public attention.

The new movie launched in a blaze of publicity.

A blaze of gunfire — A sudden, intense burst of shooting.

The soldiers were caught in a blaze of gunfire.

1849:
To blaze means to burn very brightly and strongly — not a gentle, quiet burning, but fire that is big, intense, and dramatic.

The building blazed for hours before firefighters arrived.
A log fire blazed in the living room, filling it with warmth.

Think of a roaring bonfire, not a candle. The word carries the feeling of something powerful and almost out of control. When something blazes, it doesn't just burn — it burns furiously.

Because blazing fire is so blindingly bright, the verb extended naturally to describe anything that shines with that same fierce, overwhelming brightness — especially the sun.

The sun blazed down on the desert, and there was no shade anywhere.
Stadium lights blazed across the pitch as the match began.

Here, nothing is actually on fire. But the intensity of the light feels the same. When you say "the sun blazed," you're not just saying it shone — you're saying it shone harshly, powerfully, almost aggressively.
Meaning 2: To be filled with intense emotion (especially anger)

This is where the word gets more figurative. Just as fire blazes with heat and fury, a person — or their eyes — can blaze with an intense emotion: anger, passion, excitement, or indignation. It suggests that the emotion is so strong it's almost visible, like heat radiating off a person.

Her eyes blazed with anger when she heard what he had done.
He blazed with fury at the unfair accusation.
The coach blazed at his team after the terrible performance.

The key feeling here: the emotion is not being quietly felt. It is burning, it is intense, and it shows.
Meaning 3: To shoot continuously and rapidly (guns, weapons)

When guns or weapons blaze, they are firing non-stop, rapidly, with great force — again, like fire that won't stop burning.

The soldiers' guns blazed as the battle intensified.
The fighter jet blazed through the sky, its cannons firing.

The image is one of relentless, unstoppable action.
Meaning 4: To blaze a trail (a very important special use)

This is one of the most important and commonly used forms. To blaze a trail originally had a very literal, physical meaning: when explorers walked through a dense forest, they would cut a mark (called a "blaze") into the bark of trees along the way, so others could follow the same path. So "to blaze a trail" meant to mark out a new path through unknown territory.

Over time, this became a powerful figurative expression. To blaze a trail now means to be the first to do something, to pioneer a new way, to open a path that others will follow.

Marie Curie blazed a trail for women in science.
The startup blazed a trail in electric vehicles before anyone else dared to.
He blazed a trail as the first person from his village to attend university.

From this comes the word trailblazer — a person who blazes trails, meaning a pioneer, an innovator, someone who leads the way.
Meaning 5: To spread or move very fast (especially news or fire)

When something — news, a story, a rumour, a fire — blazes through a place, it means it spreads incredibly fast, with force and intensity, the way fire races through dry grass.

The news of the arrest blazed through the small town within minutes.
Rumours blazed across the internet overnight.
The wildfire blazed through the forest, destroying everything in its path.

The feeling here is speed + intensity. It doesn't just spread — it races and consumes as it goes.
Meaning 6: To display or announce loudly and prominently

Less common but still used: when something is blazed across a headline, a screen, or a billboard, it means it is displayed in a very large, impossible-to-miss, bold way — the way a blaze of fire is impossible to ignore.

His name was blazed across the front page of every newspaper.
The scandal was blazed across every TV screen in the country.

In informal, colloquial speech (especially in North American English), to blaze or to blaze up means to smoke marijuana. This is slang, not formal usage.

"They were blazing in the park."

You'll encounter this meaning frequently in casual conversation, music, and informal writing, so it's worth knowing — but avoid it in formal contexts.

Every single meaning of "blaze" as a verb comes from one central image: fire that is intense, bright, fast, and impossible to ignore. Whether it's the sun blazing down, someone's eyes blazing with anger, a trail being blazed through a forest, or news blazing across the internet — the word always carries the feeling of something fierce, powerful, and hard to miss. Once you hold that central image in your mind, every use of this word will feel natural and logical.
